home, first visit.home: From the model to the metal. Learn the GenAI stack layer by layer, with a simulator that runs in your browser, from how a model is built down to a multi-node GPU cluster. Load real open models onto H100s and Blackwells, split them across GPUs and servers, start a Ray cluster, and fix what breaks: models that won't fit, slow tokens, idle GPUs, crashing prompts, mismatched drivers, slow networks. Start level 1 Open GPU lab Open kernel lab Each level sets up one problem. Change the hardware, precision or software with the buttons or the terminal, hit the objectives, then read how it connects to the rest of the stack. Fewer hints means more stars. Turn on Show the math any time for the formulas. $ foundry load llama-70b --dtype bf16 CUDA out of memory: needs 145.5 GB, H100 SXM has 80 GB $ foundry dtype fp8 → 74.9 / 80 GB · fits · 37.3 tok/s per user $ nvidia-smi | GPU Name | Memory-Usage | GPU-Util | | 0 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 | 71431MiB / 81559MiB | 100% | $ foundry gpu h200 && foundry context 2k && foundry batch 32 → 95.1 / 141 GB · fits · 1,335 tok/s · $0.73 per 1M tokens Where this sits in the stackThe ten layers from your GenAI stack, top to bottom. W5Kubernetes makes GPUs consumableGPU Operator, device plugin, scheduling, MIG in K8s, KubeRay, DCGM★Finale: 8 × H100 ≠ a serviceAssemble the path from GPU to API endpoint GlossaryThe words the levels use, in one place.SMStreaming MultiprocessorThe GPU's repeated building block. Kernels run as thread blocks spread across all SMs.Tensor Corematrix unitHardware inside each SM that multiplies small matrix tiles very fast. Where almost all AI math happens.HBMHigh Bandwidth MemoryThe GPU's own memory, stacked beside the die. Holds weights and KV cache.Memory capacityGBHow much fits: weights + KV cache + runtime overhead.Memory bandwidthTB/sHow fast data moves from HBM to the SMs. Usually sets tokens per second.TFLOPScomputeTrillions of math operations per second. Peak depends on precision: FP8 is about 2× BF16, FP4 about 2× FP8.PrecisionBF16 · FP8 · INT4 · FP4Bytes used to store each number. Fewer bytes: smaller and faster, with some quality risk.QuantisationoptimisationConverting a model to lower precision to save memory and time.Weight-only quantisationINT4 on HopperWeights stored in 4 bits but unpacked to 16-bit for the math. Saves memory, not compute.KV cacheper conversationSaved keys and values for every token already read, so the model doesn't redo work. Grows with users × context.Prefillphase 1Processing the whole prompt at once. Compute-bound. Sets time to first token.Decodephase 2Generating one token at a time. Memory-bound. Sets tokens per second.TTFTtime to first tokenHow long the user waits before the answer starts.BatchingthroughputServing many users in the same step so one read of the weights does more work.Arithmetic intensityFLOPs per byteHow much math a workload does for each byte it reads. Low means memory-bound.RooflinechartPlot of achievable speed against arithmetic intensity: a sloped memory roof meets a flat compute roof at the ridge.KernelGPU programOne function launched onto the GPU, such as a matrix multiply. A token needs hundreds.CUDAplatformNVIDIA's software platform for GPU computing: language, runtime, libraries and driver interface.Driverhost softwareInstalled on the machine, owns the GPU, and sets the highest CUDA version you can use.cuBLAS / CUTLASSlibrariesNVIDIA's tuned matrix-multiply kernels and the templates for building new ones.Tritonkernel languagePython-like language for writing GPU kernels; torch.compile uses it to generate fused kernels.CUDA GraphslaunchRecord a sequence of kernel launches once, replay it with one call. Removes CPU launch overhead.Kernel fusionoptimisationCombining several operations into one kernel so intermediate results stay on-chip.FlashAttentionattention kernelComputes attention in on-chip tiles so the huge score matrix never goes to HBM.Container ToolkitNVIDIALets containers see the host's GPUs and driver when started with --gpus.nvidia-smitoolCommand-line status for NVIDIA GPUs. Its GPU-Util only means 'a kernel was running', not how busy the chip is.KV-cache quantisationFP8 KVStoring the KV cache in 8 bits instead of 16. Doubles how much context fits, small accuracy risk.Mixture of expertsMoEEach token uses only a few 'expert' sub-networks. All experts must be in memory, but each token reads and computes only the active ones.Active parametersMoEParameters actually used per token. Qwen3 235B-A22B has 235B total, 22B active.Performance per watttokens per kWhWork done per unit of energy. Power and cooling, not GPU count, often limit data centres.MIGMulti-Instance GPUHardware partitioning of one GPU into isolated slices with their own compute and memory.Time-slicingGPU sharingTaking turns on the whole GPU. Simple, but no memory isolation or guaranteed share.NVLink / NVSwitchscale-upDirect GPU-to-GPU links inside a server (900 GB/s per H100) and the switch chips that connect them all.Tensor parallelismTPSplitting every layer's matrices across GPUs. Needs an all-reduce after each layer, so it wants NVLink.Pipeline parallelismPPSplitting the model by layers into stages on different GPUs or servers. Only passes activations between stages.Data parallelismDP / replicasFull copies of the model each handling different requests (inference) or different data (training).NCCLcollectivesNVIDIA's library for GPU-to-GPU communication: all-reduce, all-gather, etc., over NVLink and the network.All-reducecollectiveEvery GPU contributes a tensor and every GPU gets the sum. TP does it every layer; training does it for gradients.InfiniBandscale-out networkLow-latency, RDMA-native network for GPU clusters. NDR = 400 Gb/s per port.RoCERDMA over EthernetRDMA on Ethernet switches. Close to InfiniBand when the network is tuned for it.RDMAremote DMAOne machine's NIC writes straight into another machine's memory, without the CPUs copying data.GPUDirect RDMANVIDIAThe NIC reads and writes GPU memory directly, skipping a copy through CPU memory.Railnetwork designThe lane from GPU n in every server to the same leaf switch. Keeps most traffic to one switch hop.Raydistributed computePython framework that pools many machines' CPUs and GPUs. vLLM uses it to run one model across servers.Scaling efficiencytrainingHow close N servers get to N× the speed of one. Network time is the usual thief.ROCmAMD softwareAMD's equivalent of CUDA: compiler, runtime, libraries (rocBLAS, hipBLASLt, MIOpen) and RCCL for communication.HIPAMDC++ GPU programming interface that mirrors CUDA closely, so most CUDA code ports with mechanical changes.Compute UnitAMDAMD's building block, like an SM. Contains Matrix Cores, AMD's Tensor Cores.Infinity FabricAMD interconnectAMD's chip-to-chip and GPU-to-GPU links; the AMD counterpart to NVLink.amd-smitoolAMD's GPU status tool, the counterpart to nvidia-smi (older: rocm-smi).GB200 NVL72rack-scale72 Blackwell GPUs in one liquid-cooled rack, all on one NVLink domain: the scale-up network grows from 8 GPUs to 72.TPUGoogleGoogle's own AI accelerator. Rented only through Google Cloud; programmed via JAX/XLA or PyTorch/XLA.Trainium / InferentiaAWSAmazon's own AI chips, rented only on AWS and programmed through the Neuron SDK. Everything runs in a simplified model on this page. GPU specs are published peak figures (B200 uses its usable 180 GB), speeds assume ~80% of peak memory bandwidth and ~60% of peak compute, network and power figures are rough, and hourly prices are illustrative. Real systems differ in the details; the relationships hold. Reset progress

Wins wherever memory is the limit; no faster for prompt reading. H200 → B200: new Blackwell architecture: two dies acting as one GPU, ~2.3× FP8 math, new FP4, 8 TB/s, NVLink 5 at twice the speed, and 1,000 W. B200 → B300: Blackwell Ultra: 288 GB and more FP4 math, same bandwidth, 1,400 W and liquid cooling. Rack scale: GB200/GB300 NVL72 puts 72 GPUs on one NVLink domain instead of 8. AMD, generation by generation MI300X: CDNA 3, built from 8 compute chiplets. Its 192 GB was the most memory per GPU when it launched, at H100-class compute. MI325X: the same chip with 256 GB of HBM3e and 6 TB/s: AMD's version of the H100 → H200 step. MI355X: CDNA 4: ~2× FP8 math, FP4 and FP6, 288 GB at 8 TB/s, 1,400 W and liquid cooling. Its specs sit alongside B300. Next: the MI400 series (432 GB HBM4) and the 72-GPU Helios rack, AMD's answer to NVL72. Reading a spec sheet Match the spec to the bottleneck: memory GB for model + users, TB/s for token speed, TFLOPS for long prompts and big batches. Check whether TFLOPS are dense or sparse, and which precision. Check the GPU-to-GPU link if a model spans GPUs, and the power and cooling your racks can take. Software decides how much of the peak you actually get. Benchmark your model, on your inference engine, on both vendors. Beyond GPUs Google TPU (latest: Ironwood, 192 GB HBM per chip): built only for AI, available only in Google Cloud, joined into pods of thousands of chips. Programmed with JAX or PyTorch/XLA. AWS Trainium: Amazon's own training and inference chips, available only on AWS, programmed with the Neuron SDK. These trade portability for price and scale: your code and skills don't move to another cloud as easily.

level tokens.mission: World 0 · Level 1 Words into tokens Tokens Models don't read letters or words. They read tokens: chunks of text from a fixed vocabulary. Llama 3's vocabulary has 128,256 of them. Common words are usually one token; rare words, names and long numbers break into pieces.Everything in this game is counted in tokens: context length, speed (tokens per second) and price (dollars per million tokens).Type your own text in the box, or use tokenize … in the terminal. Find a word that splits into several tokens, and try a number or another language. Roughly:1 token ≈ ¾ of an English word, so 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words ≈ 1.5 pages.Other languages, code and numbers often take more tokens per word, so they cost more and fill the context faster.Llama 3 splits numbers into chunks of up to 3 digits, one reason models can be shaky at arithmetic.This page uses an approximation of Llama 3's rules; real tokenizers (like OpenAI's tiktoken or Hugging Face's) split slightly differently.Each token is then looked up in the model's embedding table and becomes a list of numbers. level parameters.mission: World 0 · Level 2 What's in 8 billion parameters Weights & layers A parameter (or weight) is one number the model learned in training. Llama 3.1 8B has 8.03 billion of them, arranged in big grids called matrices.The model is a stack. An embedding table turns each token into a list of 4,096 numbers. Then 32 identical layers each refine that list with two blocks: attention (tokens look at each other) and a feed-forward (MLP) block (each token is processed on its own). Finally an output head scores every token in the vocabulary to pick the next one.Tap the blocks to see their sizes. Then switch to 70B: same design, wider and deeper. Objectives Inspect an attention blockInspect a feed-forward (MLP) blockLook inside Llama 3.1 70B Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level parameters.mission: World 0 · Level 2 What's in 8 billion parameters Weights & layers A parameter (or weight) is one number the model learned in training. Llama 3.1 8B has 8.03 billion of them, arranged in big grids called matrices.The model is a stack. An embedding table turns each token into a list of 4,096 numbers. Then 32 identical layers each refine that list with two blocks: attention (tokens look at each other) and a feed-forward (MLP) block (each token is processed on its own). Finally an output head scores every token in the vocabulary to pick the next one.Tap the blocks to see their sizes. Then switch to 70B: same design, wider and deeper. Then raise the number of tokens processed at once to 32 and see how many experts get used. level moe-experts.modal: World 0 · Level 3 cleared A team of experts ★★★ Each token used only 8 of 128 experts, so it did about 22 B parameters' worth of work in a 235 B model. That's the MoE deal: the knowledge of a huge model at the speed of a much smaller one.Memory still holds everything. Any token might pick any expert, so all 235 B parameters must sit in GPU memory.Many users wake up most experts. With 32 tokens in one step, around 87% of the experts were picked by someone, so the GPU has to read most of the weights again. That's what you'll see in World 1, Level 8.Each layer has its own router and its own experts; this shows one layer of 94. Real routing is learned in training; the picks here are illustrative.Many MoE models also have a shared expert that every token uses, for knowledge everything needs.↑ UpMost frontier models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama 4, gpt-oss, Kimi) are MoE, so model choice now means choosing total vs active size.↓ DownBig MoE models spread experts across many GPUs (expert parallelism), which needs fast GPU-to-GPU links (World 3). level attention.mission: World 0 · Level 4 Who is "it"? Attention: queries, keys, values Attention is how a token gathers context from the tokens before it. Each token makes three vectors:Query: what am I looking for?Key: what do I contain?Value: what do I pass on if I'm chosen?A token compares its query with every earlier token's key. Good matches get more weight, and the token takes a weighted mix of their values.Click "it" in the sentence: which word does it look at? Then switch to head 2: each layer has many heads, each looking for something different. Finally click the first word. level attention-heads.modal: World 0 · Level 5 cleared Many heads, shared notes ★★★ Query heads cost nothing to store: a query is used once, when its token is processed. Keys and values must be kept, because every later token searches them. So the number of KV heads sets the KV cache size.Multi-head (32 KV heads): most flexible, biggest cache. About 0.5 MB per token for an 8B-sized model.Grouped-query (8): 4× smaller cache, little quality loss. Llama 3, Qwen and most current models use it.Multi-query (1): 32× smaller, but every head searches the same notes, which can cost quality.So the KV formula uses KV heads: 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × bytes.↑ UpFewer KV heads means more users or longer conversations per GPU: a cost lever chosen when the model is designed.↓ DownWorld 1, Level 3 and World 1, Level 7: the KV cache decides how many users fit. level kv-cache-basics.modal: World 0 · Level 7 cleared Notes to self ★★★ Without the cache, the model processed 68 tokens to write 8; with it, 12. For real conversations the gap is enormous: a 1,000-token answer to a 1,000-token prompt is about 1.5 million token-passes without a cache and 2,000 with one.The price is memory: every token keeps its keys and values in every layer. For Llama 3.1 70B that's ~0.33 MB per token, ~43 GB for a single 128k-token conversation.Now the GPU picture makes sense: weights are fixed and shared (blue in World 1's memory bar); the KV cache grows with every token of every user (yellow).Fewer KV heads (grouped-query attention) and FP8 KV storage both shrink it.↑ UpServing engines manage the KV cache (paging, reuse across requests, eviction): layer 5.↓ DownWorld 1, Level 3 and World 1, Level 7: the KV cache decides how many users fit on a GPU. Next: Checkpoint: inside the model Keep exploring All levels

level gpu-anatomy.mission: World 1 · Level 1 Meet the chip SMs, Tensor Cores, HBM A GPU is a package with two kinds of parts that matter for AI. In the middle is the die: silicon tiled with Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each holding Tensor Cores that do matrix math. Around it sit stacks of HBM, the GPU's own memory, where the model lives.The picture is a map of an H100 serving a small model. Tap a square in the die and a memory stack to see what they do. Run nvidia-smi, the first command every GPU operator types. Then compare with a Blackwell GPU. Objectives Run nvidia-smiInspect an SM (tap a square in the die)Inspect an HBM memory stackSwitch to a Blackwell GPU (B200 or B300) Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level gpu-anatomy.mission: World 1 · Level 1 Meet the chip SMs, Tensor Cores, HBM A GPU is a package with two kinds of parts that matter for AI. In the middle is the die: silicon tiled with Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each holding Tensor Cores that do matrix math. Around it sit stacks of HBM, the GPU's own memory, where the model lives.The picture is a map of an H100 serving a small model. Tap a square in the die and a memory stack to see what they do. Run nvidia-smi, the first command every GPU operator types. Then compare with a Blackwell GPU. Objectives Run nvidia-smiInspect an SM (tap a square in the die)Inspect an HBM memory stackSwitch to a Blackwell GPU (B200 or B300) Hints Show the answer Type nvidia-smi in the terminal and press Run.Tap any small square inside the dark die, then any block beside it. Or type foundry inspect sm and foundry inspect hbm.Pick B200 in the GPU buttons, or type foundry gpu b200.Answer: nvidia-smi && foundry inspect sm && foundry inspect hbm && foundry gpu b200 Use it Restart level Command list Glossary

INT4 also fits, but with a bigger quality risk you'd need to test on your own tasks.BF16 needs ~141 GB. Even an H200 (141 GB) can't hold it plus a KV cache. A B200 can.Hopper's Tensor Cores run FP8 math natively, and FP8 is usually very close to BF16 quality.In real life: vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct --quantization fp8.↑ UpModel optimisation (layer 7) is where quantisation lives, and the model layer (6) decides parameter count. Both turn directly into GB on this chip.↓ DownIf no precision fits, you split the model across several GPUs connected by NVLink (World 3). Next: Room to talk Keep exploring All levels

level memory-bandwidth.modal: World 1 · Level 4 cleared Fast chip, slow tokens ★★★ The H200 has identical compute to the H100 but 43% more bandwidth, and it produced tokens 43% faster. Generating tokens one at a time is memory-bound.Tokens/s per user ≈ bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token. That's why each new HBM generation matters so much for inference.On the roofline your workload sits far left, on the sloped memory roof. The flat compute roof is out of reach with one user.nvidia-smi said GPU-Util 100% while the Tensor Cores were under 1% busy. Tools like NVIDIA DCGM report Tensor Core activity instead (World 5).↑ UpLatency targets in the application (1) and model routing in the gateway (3) depend on this number. A 'fast' tier is often a high-bandwidth GPU or a smaller model.↓ DownQuantisation (layer 7) helps here too: fewer bytes per weight means fewer bytes to read per token. level batching.modal: World 1 · Level 5 cleared Fill the factory ★★★ One read of the weights now serves many users, so total throughput rose almost in step with batch size while each user slowed only a little. Cost per token fell by more than 20×.The ceiling was KV cache memory, not compute. Around 100 users at 2k context, the H200 runs out.On the roofline the point moved right: more math for every byte read.Real engines do this all the time (continuous batching): new requests join the running batch every step. That's the inference layer's main job.↑ UpThis is the economics behind 'maximise useful AI work per unit of compute'. The serving and gateway layers exist largely to keep batches full.↓ DownPush batches large enough and you finally hit the compute roof. Then Tensor Core speed, FP8 and FP4 start to matter. level prefill-decode.mission: World 1 · Level 6 Two speeds Prefill vs decode A legal team pastes a 16,000-token contract and asks a question. The answer streams fine, but the first word takes 2.5 seconds to appear. They want time to first token at most 1.5 s.Inference has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass: thousands of tokens share each weight read, so it's limited by compute. Decode then produces one token at a time, limited by memory bandwidth.Try the H200 trick from World 1, Level 4 first and see what happens.prefill math ≈ 2 × params × prompt tokens (+ attention) = 2 × 70.6 B × 16,384 = 2.3 PFLOP time ≈ 2.3 PFLOP ÷ (1,979 TFLOPS × 65%) ≈ 1.8 s (+0.7 s attention) Objectives Time to first token at most 1.5 sEach user still gets at least 40 tokens/sEverything fits in memory Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level prefill-decode.modal: World 1 · Level 6 cleared Two speeds ★★★ The H200 didn't help: it has the same Tensor Cores as the H100. Blackwell roughly doubles FP8 math and adds FP4, so prefill got about twice as fast.Prefill is compute-bound: TFLOPS matter. Decode is memory-bound: TB/s matter. Different GPUs win different phases.INT4 on Hopper made prefill slower. The weights are stored in 4 bits, but the math still runs in 16-bit.Large deployments now run the two phases on separate GPU pools (disaggregated serving).↑ UpTTFT is the first thing users feel. RAG apps (layer 4) that stuff long retrieved context into prompts are prefill-heavy.↓ DownLong prompts also stress the attention kernels. World 2 shows how FlashAttention keeps them from blowing up memory. Next: Long memories Keep exploring All levels

level prefill-decode.mission: World 1 · Level 6 Two speeds Prefill vs decode A legal team pastes a 16,000-token contract and asks a question. The answer streams fine, but the first word takes 2.5 seconds to appear. They want time to first token at most 1.5 s.Inference has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass: thousands of tokens share each weight read, so it's limited by compute. Decode then produces one token at a time, limited by memory bandwidth.Try the H200 trick from World 1, Level 4 first and see what happens.prefill math ≈ 2 × params × prompt tokens (+ attention) = 2 × 70.6 B × 16,384 = 2.3 PFLOP time ≈ 2.3 PFLOP ÷ (1,979 TFLOPS × 65%) ≈ 1.8 s (+0.7 s attention) Objectives Time to first token at most 1.5 sEach user still gets at least 40 tokens/sEverything fits in memory Hints Show the answer Try H200: time to first token barely moves. Prefill is limited by math, not memory.You need more TFLOPS. H100 and H200 share the same compute; Blackwell roughly doubles it.Answer: foundry gpu b200 Use it Restart level Command list Glossary

level kv-quantisation.mission: World 1 · Level 7 Long memories KV-cache quantisation A research tool lets 8 analysts each keep a 32,768-token conversation going. On the H200 the KV cache alone needs 86 GB, so it doesn't fit next to the weights.Weights aren't the only thing you can store in fewer bits. The KV cache can be kept in FP8 instead of 16-bit, halving it. Accuracy usually holds up well, but it's a real trade-off worth testing on long documents.Make it fit without dropping the weights below FP8.KV cache = 8 users × 32,768 tokens × 0.33 MB = 85.9 GB (16-bit) = 8 users × 32,768 tokens × 0.16 MB = 42.9 GB (FP8) Objectives 8 users × 32,768 tokens fit on the H200Weights stay at FP8 or BF16 Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level kv-quantisation.modal: World 1 · Level 7 cleared Long memories ★★★ FP8 KV cache halved the conversation memory, from 86 GB to 43 GB, so everything fits with room to spare. It also made each token a little faster: less KV to read per step.At long context the KV cache, not the weights, is the memory hog. Quantising it is now standard in vLLM and TensorRT-LLM (--kv-cache-dtype fp8).Other tricks attack the same problem: grouped-query attention (fewer KV heads, already in Llama 3), sliding windows, and offloading old KV to CPU memory or SSD.Quality risk is real but usually small; long-document benchmarks are where to check.↑ UpContext length is a product decision (layer 1) that the serving layer (5) pays for in GB. KV quantisation is an optimisation (7) that changes the price.↓ DownLess KV to read also means less memory bandwidth per token, which you met in World 1, Level 4. level kv-quantisation.mission: World 1 · Level 7 Long memories KV-cache quantisation A research tool lets 8 analysts each keep a 32,768-token conversation going. On the H200 the KV cache alone needs 86 GB, so it doesn't fit next to the weights.Weights aren't the only thing you can store in fewer bits. The KV cache can be kept in FP8 instead of 16-bit, halving it. Accuracy usually holds up well, but it's a real trade-off worth testing on long documents.Make it fit without dropping the weights below FP8.KV cache = 8 users × 32,768 tokens × 0.33 MB = 85.9 GB (16-bit) = 8 users × 32,768 tokens × 0.16 MB = 42.9 GB (FP8) Objectives 8 users × 32,768 tokens fit on the H200Weights stay at FP8 or BF16 Hints Show the answer The yellow KV cache is bigger than the blue weights. Which of the two can you shrink without touching weight precision?Use the KV cache buttons, or foundry kv fp8.Answer: foundry kv fp8 Use it Restart level Command list Glossary

level moe-on-gpu.mission: World 1 · Level 8 Many experts Mixture of experts (MoE) Leadership wants a frontier-scale model (200B+ parameters) on a single GPU, answering at 60+ tokens/s per user, at FP8 quality.Llama 3.1 405B is dense: every token uses every weight. Qwen3 235B-A22B is a mixture of experts: each layer has 128 small "expert" networks and a router that sends each token to just 8 of them. All 235B parameters must sit in memory, but each token only reads and computes about 22B.(World 0, Level 3 shows how the router picks experts.) Find a GPU and model that hit the target. Then try 32 users and see what happens to MoE's speed advantage.dense 405B, FP8: read 406 GB per token MoE 235B-A22B: read ~22 GB per token (8 of 128 experts) 32 users: 1 − (120/128)³² = 87% of experts get used every step Objectives A 200B+ model fits on one GPU at FP8 or BF16Try 32 or more users on the MoE modelEach user gets at least 60 tokens/s Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level moe-on-gpu.mission: World 1 · Level 8 Many experts Mixture of experts (MoE) Leadership wants a frontier-scale model (200B+ parameters) on a single GPU, answering at 60+ tokens/s per user, at FP8 quality.Llama 3.1 405B is dense: every token uses every weight. Qwen3 235B-A22B is a mixture of experts: each layer has 128 small "expert" networks and a router that sends each token to just 8 of them. All 235B parameters must sit in memory, but each token only reads and computes about 22B.(World 0, Level 3 shows how the router picks experts.) Find a GPU and model that hit the target. Then try 32 users and see what happens to MoE's speed advantage.dense 405B, FP8: read 406 GB per token MoE 235B-A22B: read ~22 GB per token (8 of 128 experts) 32 users: 1 − (120/128)³² = 87% of experts get used every step Objectives A 200B+ model fits on one GPU at FP8 or BF16Try 32 or more users on the MoE modelEach user gets at least 60 tokens/s Hints Show the answer 405B in FP8 is 406 GB: no single GPU holds it. Switch to the Qwen3 MoE model.235 GB at FP8 needs the B300's 288 GB. After trying 32 users, come back down to 8 or fewer.Answer: foundry load qwen-235b && foundry gpu b300 && foundry batch 32 && foundry batch 4 Use it Restart level Command list Glossary

Each generation does more work per watt, and that, more than raw speed, is what lets a data centre grow inside its power budget.The B300 was worse per watt here: same memory bandwidth as the B200 but a higher power rating, on a workload limited by bandwidth. Its extra memory and FP4 math only pay off on workloads that use them.FP4 on the B200 would reach ~36M tokens per kWh: quantisation is an energy lever too.Above ~1,000 W per GPU, racks move to direct liquid cooling (B300, GB200 NVL72). level gpu-sharing.mission: World 1 · Level 10 Share the GPU MIG & time-slicing Five teams each need a small model, and you have one H100. Giving each team a whole GPU would waste most of it.Two ways to share. Time-slicing lets everyone take turns on the whole GPU: easy, but one team can fill the memory or hog the SMs and hurt the others. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) cuts the H100 into up to 7 isolated GPUs, each with its own SMs, memory and bandwidth.An H100 has 7 compute slices and 8 memory slices of 10 GB. Profiles are named by both, such as 1g.10gb or 2g.20gb. Turn on MIG mode, then pick a layout where every team gets its own instance that fits. level gpu-sharing.modal: World 1 · Level 10 cleared Share the GPU ★★★ One H100 now behaves like five smaller GPUs. Each team has its own memory and SMs, so a runaway job in one can't crash or slow the others.The cost of MIG is rigidity: layouts follow fixed profiles, and changing them means draining the GPU. Pieces that don't match the profiles get stranded.Time-slicing is more flexible but gives no isolation. Fine for dev notebooks, risky for production.In Kubernetes, the GPU Operator can apply MIG layouts and each instance shows up as its own resource (World 5).↑ UpPlatform teams use MIG to give many small apps (layers 1–4) a guaranteed slice of GPU without buying a GPU each.↓ DownMIG is enforced in hardware: the SMs, L2 cache and memory controllers are physically divided. level amd-gpus.modal: World 1 · Level 11 cleared Team red ★★★ The MI300X's 192 GB holds the model and all 32 conversations on one GPU, at a lower hourly price than an H200 that can't fit it.AMD's pitch has been more memory per GPU at a lower price. MI325X (256 GB) and MI355X (288 GB) continue that.The real question is software. ROCm (HIP, hipBLASLt, RCCL, MIOpen) mirrors CUDA, and vLLM, SGLang and PyTorch support it, but kernel tuning and new-model support often land on CUDA first. This game assumes equally good software on both; in practice, benchmark your own model.Operationally it's a different toolbox: amd-smi instead of nvidia-smi, ROCm container images, the AMD GPU Operator on Kubernetes.↑ UpEngines like vLLM hide most vendor differences from the application, if your model and features are supported on ROCm.↓ DownWorld 2's whole software path has an AMD twin: HIP for CUDA, hipBLASLt for cuBLAS, RCCL for NCCL, the amdgpu driver for NVIDIA's. level amd-gpus.mission: World 1 · Level 11 Team red AMD Instinct & ROCm The analytics team wants Llama 3.1 70B for 32 people with 8k-token conversations, on one GPU, and the budget is $3 per GPU-hour. That's 71 GB of weights plus 86 GB of KV cache: no Hopper GPU holds it, and Blackwell is over budget.A cloud provider offers AMD Instinct GPUs. AMD builds its GPUs from chiplets: 8 small compute dies (XCDs) full of Compute Units, AMD's equivalent of SMs, surrounded by 8 HBM stacks. The software stack is ROCm instead of CUDA.Find a GPU that fits within budget with at least 25 tokens/s per user. Then check it the AMD way: nvidia-smi won't work, amd-smi will. Objectives Everything fits on one GPUAt least 25 tokens/s per userGPU costs no more than $3.00/hrCheck the GPU with amd-smi Hints Show the answer You need about 160 GB on one GPU. For each workload, find a GPU that meets every requirement, then lock it in with foundry pick.There's no single best GPU. level software-path.mission: World 2 · Level 1 Follow one matmul The software path Model code says something simple: y = x @ W. The GPU only understands kernels, small programs launched across its SMs. Several layers of software turn one into the other.Run foundry trace matmul to follow one matrix multiply from Python down to the Tensor Cores. Then open the kernel libraries and NVIDIA driver rows to see who owns what. level software-path.modal: World 2 · Level 1 cleared Follow one matmul ★★★ One line of Python went through five layers of software before it touched silicon:PyTorch decides what to compute and routes it to the CUDA backend.Kernel libraries (cuBLAS, CUTLASS, FlashAttention, Triton-generated code) hold the hand-tuned kernels. Most of the performance lives here.The CUDA runtime ships inside your container. The driver lives on the host. That split causes the classic failure in World 2, Level 4.↑ UpInference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) sit on top of this path. They differ mostly in which kernels they use and how they schedule them.↓ DownAt the bottom, each kernel becomes thread blocks on SMs reading HBM: World 1's chip. level launch-overhead.modal: World 2 · Level 2 cleared Waiting on the CPU ★★★ CUDA Graphs record the whole sequence of kernels once, then replay it with one launch. The CPU stops being the bottleneck and the gaps disappear.Launch overhead matters most for small models and small batches, where kernels are tiny. The 8B model's bigger kernels hid much of it.Kernel fusion helped a little on its own: fewer, bigger kernels means fewer launches.In practice vLLM captures CUDA Graphs for decode by default, and torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead") uses them too.↑ UpModel benchmarks hide this, but users feel it as latency. Inference engines handle it so application teams don't have to.↓ DownThis is one case where nvidia-smi's GPU-Util is honest: it shows the gaps as a low number. level kernel-fusion.modal: World 2 · Level 3 cleared The 32k prompt ★★★ FlashAttention turned an impossible 64 GiB allocation into nothing by keeping the work on-chip.This is kernel fusion at its most dramatic: several steps combined so intermediate results stay in fast on-chip memory instead of round-tripping through HBM.Fusing the small ops (norms, activations) saved only tens of milliseconds here. level driver-stack.mission: World 2 · Level 4 Driver says no Driver, CUDA & containers A teammate shipped a new serving image built on CUDA 13.0. On your GPU server it starts, then PyTorch reports the driver is too old.Two pieces must agree. The NVIDIA driver is installed on the host. The CUDA runtime and libraries ship inside the container image. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit connects them when you start a container with --gpus all. level hgx-board.modal: World 3 · Level 1 cleared Meet the HGX board ★★★ You've seen the two speeds inside a server: tiny messages are limited by latency (microseconds per hop), big ones by bandwidth (the busbw column approaching ~450 GB/s each way).NCCL is the library every framework uses for GPU-to-GPU communication. all_reduce_perf from nccl-tests is the standard health check for a new server or cluster.All-reduce: every GPU contributes a tensor and every GPU ends up with the sum. Tensor parallelism does one after every layer."NV18" in the topology means every pair of GPUs has a full NVLink path. On a PCIe server you'd see PIX, NODE or SYS instead: slower paths through switches and CPUs.Other boards differ mainly in this fabric. HGX B200 doubles NVLink to 1.8 TB/s per GPU. AMD's 8 × MI300X board wires GPUs in a direct mesh with no switch. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 stretches one NVLink domain across 72 GPUs in a rack. Try them in the Server lab.↑ UpInference engines use NCCL under the hood whenever a model spans GPUs; you rarely call it directly.↓ DownNVLink is the scale-up network. Between servers you need a scale-out network: World 4. Next: Too big for one Keep exploring All levels

On the PCIe server (try it in the Server lab), communication eats two-thirds of every TP 8 step and smaller TP groups win.It also depends on the model and target. A model that fits comfortably on one GPU with room for KV cache is usually best served as many small replicas.Production teams sweep these settings per model and per GPU type, often with the inference engine's benchmark tools.↑ UpThe gateway (layer 3) can route traffic across replicas; the serving layer (5) decides TP size per replica.↓ DownAcross servers the same trade-off appears with a much slower network: World 4. level tp-vs-replicas.mission: World 3 · Level 4 Shards or replicas? TP size vs replicas Back to Llama 3.1 70B on one HGX server. You can run 8 replicas (TP 1), 4 × TP 2, 2 × TP 4 or 1 × TP 8. The batch slider sets users per replica.Fewer, bigger shards pay more NVLink traffic but leave far more memory for KV cache, so each replica can batch more users. More replicas avoid communication but each one is cramped.Hit at least 8,000 tokens/s for the whole server while every user still gets at least 60 tokens/s. level fabric.mission: World 4 · Level 1 Meet the fabric InfiniBand, RDMA & rails Inside a server, GPUs use NVLink. Between servers, each GPU gets its own network card: a 400 Gb/s NIC per GPU, eight per server. Each NIC is a rail: GPU 1 of every server plugs into the same leaf switch, GPU 2 into the next, and leaves connect through spine switches.Most AI clusters run InfiniBand or RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE). RDMA lets one machine's NIC write straight into another machine's memory without the CPUs copying data.You're logged into node-1. Check the NICs with ibstat, measure the link to node-2 with ib_write_bw, and tap a NIC and a leaf switch in the diagram. Objectives Check NIC status (ibstat)Measure bandwidth to node-2 (ib_write_bw node-2)Inspect a NICInspect a leaf switch Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

level fabric.modal: World 4 · Level 1 cleared Meet the fabric ★★★ One NIC gave ~390 Gb/s, close to its 400 Gb/s line rate. Eight of them give each server about 400 GB/s to the rest of the cluster.That sounds like a lot, but per GPU it's 50 GB/s against NVLink's 450 GB/s. Crossing a server boundary is ~9× slower per GPU, and adds microseconds of latency per hop.That gap is the single most important fact for multi-node design: keep the chattiest traffic inside the server.Rail-optimised wiring means GPU n in one server usually reaches GPU n in another through a single switch.↑ UpTraining clusters and multi-node inference both live or die by this network.↓ DownPhysically: optical cables, transceivers and switches, often a major share of cluster cost and power. level fabric.mission: World 4 · Level 1 Meet the fabric InfiniBand, RDMA & rails Inside a server, GPUs use NVLink. Between servers, each GPU gets its own network card: a 400 Gb/s NIC per GPU, eight per server. Each NIC is a rail: GPU 1 of every server plugs into the same leaf switch, GPU 2 into the next, and leaves connect through spine switches.Most AI clusters run InfiniBand or RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE). RDMA lets one machine's NIC write straight into another machine's memory without the CPUs copying data.You're logged into node-1. Check the NICs with ibstat, measure the link to node-2 with ib_write_bw, and tap a NIC and a leaf switch in the diagram. Ray pooled 16 GPUs, and vLLM used tensor parallelism inside each server (TP 8 over NVLink) and pipeline parallelism across servers (PP 2: layers 1–63 on node-1, 64–126 on node-2).Ray is a general distributed-computing framework: the same cluster can run training (Ray Train), batch inference (Ray Data) and serving (Ray Serve).The head node is a single point of control; production setups add monitoring and restart policies.On Kubernetes, KubeRay creates Ray clusters as Kubernetes objects (World 5). Slurm is the HPC alternative, common for training.↑ UpTo the gateway this is still one endpoint, just a 16-GPU one.↓ DownPipeline stages hand activations to each other over InfiniBand, once per stage per step. level pipeline-parallel.modal: World 4 · Level 3 cleared Split the right way ★★★ The rule of thumb: TP size = GPUs per server, PP size = number of servers. Chatty traffic stays on NVLink; only one hand-off per stage crosses the network.TP 16 actually had slightly faster decode (each GPU read less), but its prefill all-reduces crossed InfiniBand 252 times and doubled first-token time.TP 4 × PP 4 kept traffic local but made every token walk through 4 stages in turn: slow decode.Pipeline parallelism shines for throughput: different requests can occupy different stages at once.↑ UpLayout is a serving-layer (5) setting, but choosing it well needs to know the network (10).↓ DownEven PP's hand-offs need RDMA to be quick. level data-parallel.mission: World 4 · Level 4 Train across racks Data parallel training Training is the network's hardest test. In data-parallel training, every GPU processes different data, then all GPUs all-reduce their gradients, every step: 16 GB for an 8B model.The research team is fine-tuning Llama 3.1 8B on 4 servers (32 GPUs), but the cluster was built on plain 100G Ethernet. 4 servers run barely faster than 2.Get scaling efficiency to at least 95% on 4 nodes: 4 servers should do ≥95% of 4× the work of one. Choose the network, and decide whether to use GPUDirect RDMA, which lets NICs read GPU memory directly instead of copying through the CPU. What does RDMA let a NIC do?Compress dataWrite directly into another machine's memory without the CPUs copying itRun CUDA kernelsEncrypt the modelRDMA cuts out CPU copies and kernel overhead, giving low latency and high throughput. GPUDirect RDMA extends it to GPU memory.3. You need 16 GPUs across 2 servers for one model. The usual layout is…TP 16 across both serversTP 8 inside each server, PP 2 across serversPP 16Two independent replicasTensor parallelism all-reduces every layer, so it belongs on NVLink. Pipeline stages only hand off activations once per stage.4. What does ray start --address=node-1:6379 do on node-2?Starts a new head nodeJoins node-2's CPUs and GPUs to the Ray cluster headed by node-1Downloads the modelOpens port 6379 to the internet5. Data-parallel training scaling efficiency drops from 96% to 40% when you move from 400G RDMA to one 100G Ethernet NIC per server. sweep in gpu-anatomy.mission: World 1 · Level 1 Meet the chip SMs, Tensor Cores, HBM A GPU is a package with two kinds of parts that matter for AI. In the middle is the die: silicon tiled with Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each holding Tensor Cores that do matrix math. Around it sit stacks of HBM, the GPU's own memory, where the model lives.The picture is a map of an H100 serving a small model. Tap a square in the die and a memory stack to see what they do. Run nvidia-smi, the first command every GPU operator types. Then compare with a Blackwell GPU. sweep in gpu-anatomy.mission: World 1 · Level 1 Meet the chip SMs, Tensor Cores, HBM A GPU is a package with two kinds of parts that matter for AI. In the middle is the die: silicon tiled with Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), each holding Tensor Cores that do matrix math. Around it sit stacks of HBM, the GPU's own memory, where the model lives.The picture is a map of an H100 serving a small model. Tap a square in the die and a memory stack to see what they do. Run nvidia-smi, the first command every GPU operator types. Then compare with a Blackwell GPU. sweep in launch-overhead.mission: World 2 · Level 2 Waiting on the CPU Launch overhead & CUDA Graphs A small model, Llama 3.2 1B, runs on an H100 for one user. It should be blazing fast, but the GPU sits idle most of the time.The CPU launches every kernel. See the hatched gaps on the timeline.Look at Llama 3.1 8B once to compare. Then, on the 1B model, get the GPU at least 85% busy and a token every 1.8 ms or less. sweep in hgx-board.modal: World 3 · Level 1 cleared Meet the HGX board ★★★ You've seen the two speeds inside a server: tiny messages are limited by latency (microseconds per hop), big ones by bandwidth (the busbw column approaching ~450 GB/s each way).NCCL is the library every framework uses for GPU-to-GPU communication. all_reduce_perf from nccl-tests is the standard health check for a new server or cluster.All-reduce: every GPU contributes a tensor and every GPU ends up with the sum. Tensor parallelism does one after every layer."NV18" in the topology means every pair of GPUs has a full NVLink path. On a PCIe server you'd see PIX, NODE or SYS instead: slower paths through switches and CPUs.Other boards differ mainly in this fabric. HGX B200 doubles NVLink to 1.8 TB/s per GPU. AMD's 8 × MI300X board wires GPUs in a direct mesh with no switch. NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 stretches one NVLink domain across 72 GPUs in a rack. Try them in the Server lab.↑ UpInference engines use NCCL under the hood whenever a model spans GPUs; you rarely call it directly.↓ DownNVLink is the scale-up network. Between servers you need a scale-out network: World 4. Next: Too big for one Keep exploring All levels

Between servers, each GPU gets its own network card: a 400 Gb/s NIC per GPU, eight per server. Each NIC is a rail: GPU 1 of every server plugs into the same leaf switch, GPU 2 into the next, and leaves connect through spine switches.Most AI clusters run InfiniBand or RDMA-capable Ethernet (RoCE). RDMA lets one machine's NIC write straight into another machine's memory without the CPUs copying data.You're logged into node-1. Check the NICs with ibstat, measure the link to node-2 with ib_write_bw, and tap a NIC and a leaf switch in the diagram. Objectives Check NIC status (ibstat)Measure bandwidth to node-2 (ib_write_bw node-2)Inspect a NICInspect a leaf switch Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

test2: Ray cluster mistakes.mission: World 4 · Level 2 Two boxes, one model Ray clusters & multi-node The team wants Llama 3.1 405B in BF16, no quantisation: 812 GB. One HGX H100 server has 640 GB, so it takes two servers.Something has to make two machines act as one pool of GPUs. Ray does that: start a head node, have the other machine join it, and Ray sees 16 GPUs. vLLM then uses Ray to place one model across them.You're on node-1. Start Ray, ssh node-2 and join it to the cluster, check ray status, then launch the model across 16 GPUs from the head node.node-1$ ray start --head --port=6379 node-2$ ray start --address=node-1:6379 node-1$ vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 --pipeline-parallel-size 2 \ --distributed-executor-backend ray Objectives Start the Ray head on node-1node-2 joins the clusterray status shows 16 GPUs405B BF16 is serving across 16 GPUs Hints Show a hint Restart level Command list Glossary

test2: MIG mistakes.mission: World 1 · Level 10 Share the GPU MIG & time-slicing Five teams each need a small model, and you have one H100. Giving each team a whole GPU would waste most of it.Two ways to share. Time-slicing lets everyone take turns on the whole GPU: easy, but one team can fill the memory or hog the SMs and hurt the others. MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) cuts the H100 into up to 7 isolated GPUs, each with its own SMs, memory and bandwidth.An H100 has 7 compute slices and 8 memory slices of 10 GB. Profiles are named by both, such as 1g.10gb or 2g.20gb. Turn on MIG mode, then pick a layout where every team gets its own instance that fits. home, after playing everything.home: From the model to the metal. Learn the GenAI stack layer by layer, with a simulator that runs in your browser, from how a model is built down to a multi-node GPU cluster. Load real open models onto H100s and Blackwells, split them across GPUs and servers, start a Ray cluster, and fix what breaks: models that won't fit, slow tokens, idle GPUs, crashing prompts, mismatched drivers, slow networks. Replay level 1 Open GPU lab Open kernel lab Each level sets up one problem. Change the hardware, precision or software with the buttons or the terminal, hit the objectives, then read how it connects to the rest of the stack. Fewer hints means more stars. Turn on Show the math any time for the formulas. $ foundry load llama-70b --dtype bf16 CUDA out of memory: needs 145.5 GB, H100 SXM has 80 GB $ foundry dtype fp8 → 74.9 / 80 GB · fits · 37.3 tok/s per user $ nvidia-smi | GPU Name | Memory-Usage | GPU-Util | | 0 NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 | 71431MiB / 81559MiB | 100% | $ foundry gpu h200 && foundry context 2k && foundry batch 32 → 95.1 / 141 GB · fits · 1,335 tok/s · $0.73 per 1M tokens Where this sits in the stackThe ten layers from your GenAI stack, top to bottom. W5Kubernetes makes GPUs consumableGPU Operator, device plugin, scheduling, MIG in K8s, KubeRay, DCGM★Finale: 8 × H100 ≠ a serviceAssemble the path from GPU to API endpoint GlossaryThe words the levels use, in one place.SMStreaming MultiprocessorThe GPU's repeated building block. Kernels run as thread blocks spread across all SMs.Tensor Corematrix unitHardware inside each SM that multiplies small matrix tiles very fast. Where almost all AI math happens.HBMHigh Bandwidth MemoryThe GPU's own memory, stacked beside the die. Holds weights and KV cache.Memory capacityGBHow much fits: weights + KV cache + runtime overhead.Memory bandwidthTB/sHow fast data moves from HBM to the SMs. Usually sets tokens per second.TFLOPScomputeTrillions of math operations per second. Peak depends on precision: FP8 is about 2× BF16, FP4 about 2× FP8.PrecisionBF16 · FP8 · INT4 · FP4Bytes used to store each number. Fewer bytes: smaller and faster, with some quality risk.QuantisationoptimisationConverting a model to lower precision to save memory and time.Weight-only quantisationINT4 on HopperWeights stored in 4 bits but unpacked to 16-bit for the math. Saves memory, not compute.KV cacheper conversationSaved keys and values for every token already read, so the model doesn't redo work. Grows with users × context.Prefillphase 1Processing the whole prompt at once. Compute-bound. Sets time to first token.Decodephase 2Generating one token at a time. Memory-bound. Sets tokens per second.TTFTtime to first tokenHow long the user waits before the answer starts.BatchingthroughputServing many users in the same step so one read of the weights does more work.Arithmetic intensityFLOPs per byteHow much math a workload does for each byte it reads. Low means memory-bound.RooflinechartPlot of achievable speed against arithmetic intensity: a sloped memory roof meets a flat compute roof at the ridge.KernelGPU programOne function launched onto the GPU, such as a matrix multiply. A token needs hundreds.CUDAplatformNVIDIA's software platform for GPU computing: language, runtime, libraries and driver interface.Driverhost softwareInstalled on the machine, owns the GPU, and sets the highest CUDA version you can use.cuBLAS / CUTLASSlibrariesNVIDIA's tuned matrix-multiply kernels and the templates for building new ones.Tritonkernel languagePython-like language for writing GPU kernels; torch.compile uses it to generate fused kernels.CUDA GraphslaunchRecord a sequence of kernel launches once, replay it with one call. Removes CPU launch overhead.Kernel fusionoptimisationCombining several operations into one kernel so intermediate results stay on-chip.FlashAttentionattention kernelComputes attention in on-chip tiles so the huge score matrix never goes to HBM.Container ToolkitNVIDIALets containers see the host's GPUs and driver when started with --gpus.nvidia-smitoolCommand-line status for NVIDIA GPUs. Its GPU-Util only means 'a kernel was running', not how busy the chip is.KV-cache quantisationFP8 KVStoring the KV cache in 8 bits instead of 16. Doubles how much context fits, small accuracy risk.Mixture of expertsMoEEach token uses only a few 'expert' sub-networks. All experts must be in memory, but each token reads and computes only the active ones.Active parametersMoEParameters actually used per token. Qwen3 235B-A22B has 235B total, 22B active.Performance per watttokens per kWhWork done per unit of energy. Power and cooling, not GPU count, often limit data centres.MIGMulti-Instance GPUHardware partitioning of one GPU into isolated slices with their own compute and memory.Time-slicingGPU sharingTaking turns on the whole GPU. Simple, but no memory isolation or guaranteed share.NVLink / NVSwitchscale-upDirect GPU-to-GPU links inside a server (900 GB/s per H100) and the switch chips that connect them all.Tensor parallelismTPSplitting every layer's matrices across GPUs. Needs an all-reduce after each layer, so it wants NVLink.Pipeline parallelismPPSplitting the model by layers into stages on different GPUs or servers. Only passes activations between stages.Data parallelismDP / replicasFull copies of the model each handling different requests (inference) or different data (training).NCCLcollectivesNVIDIA's library for GPU-to-GPU communication: all-reduce, all-gather, etc., over NVLink and the network.All-reducecollectiveEvery GPU contributes a tensor and every GPU gets the sum. TP does it every layer; training does it for gradients.InfiniBandscale-out networkLow-latency, RDMA-native network for GPU clusters. NDR = 400 Gb/s per port.RoCERDMA over EthernetRDMA on Ethernet switches. Close to InfiniBand when the network is tuned for it.RDMAremote DMAOne machine's NIC writes straight into another machine's memory, without the CPUs copying data.GPUDirect RDMANVIDIAThe NIC reads and writes GPU memory directly, skipping a copy through CPU memory.Railnetwork designThe lane from GPU n in every server to the same leaf switch. Keeps most traffic to one switch hop.Raydistributed computePython framework that pools many machines' CPUs and GPUs. vLLM uses it to run one model across servers.Scaling efficiencytrainingHow close N servers get to N× the speed of one. Network time is the usual thief.ROCmAMD softwareAMD's equivalent of CUDA: compiler, runtime, libraries (rocBLAS, hipBLASLt, MIOpen) and RCCL for communication.HIPAMDC++ GPU programming interface that mirrors CUDA closely, so most CUDA code ports with mechanical changes.Compute UnitAMDAMD's building block, like an SM. Contains Matrix Cores, AMD's Tensor Cores.Infinity FabricAMD interconnectAMD's chip-to-chip and GPU-to-GPU links; the AMD counterpart to NVLink.amd-smitoolAMD's GPU status tool, the counterpart to nvidia-smi (older: rocm-smi).GB200 NVL72rack-scale72 Blackwell GPUs in one liquid-cooled rack, all on one NVLink domain: the scale-up network grows from 8 GPUs to 72.TPUGoogleGoogle's own AI accelerator. Rented only through Google Cloud; programmed via JAX/XLA or PyTorch/XLA.Trainium / InferentiaAWSAmazon's own AI chips, rented only on AWS and programmed through the Neuron SDK. Everything runs in a simplified model on this page. GPU specs are published peak figures (B200 uses its usable 180 GB), speeds assume ~80% of peak memory bandwidth and ~60% of peak compute, network and power figures are rough, and hourly prices are illustrative. Real systems differ in the details; the relationships hold. Reset progress
